title: GameVerse: A Minute-Scale Gameplay Dataset for Long-Horizon Interactive World Modeling
summary: Recent advances in interactive world models have made it possible to generate controllable, dynamic environments from action inputs. Yet current models struggle to maintain coherence beyond roughly one minute of rollout, a limitation rooted not in model capacity but in the scarcity of long-horizon training data. Existing gameplay video datasets typically consist of clips under ten seconds, with captions that describe whole clips in coarse and undifferentiated text, which is insufficient for controllable long-horizon generation. We address this with GameVerse, a minute-scale gameplay video dataset purpose-built for long-horizon interactive world modeling. GameVerse contains 69.7K clips spanning 1,655 hours and 349.6 million frames across diverse first- and third-person gameplay, including 1,358 hours of continuous two-minute sequences, an order of magnitude longer than prior datasets. Clips pass through a unified pipeline of scene-consistent segmentation, quality filtering, camera pose estimation, and event-based caption annotation. Each clip is paired with a temporally stable camera trajectory that remains coherent across minutes, together with captions that separate static scene context from dynamic foreground events and align to event boundaries rather than fixed time windows. Comprehensive analysis shows that GameVerse surpasses existing public datasets in scale, diversity, and annotation quality. Experiments further demonstrate that training on GameVerse substantially extends the temporal horizon of interactive world models.

title: Agentic Distributional Regression: Conditional Density Estimation through Agent-Written Programs
summary: Artificial intelligence offers statisticians a new paradigm for modelling and analysing complex datasets. Agents based on large language models can reason about data and automate key stages of the statistical modelling workflow, from model fitting to validation. In this paper we propose a method that uses such an agent to estimate the conditional density of a response given a vector of covariates from an iid sample. The agent examines the sample, chooses a model for the conditional distribution of the response and the procedure to fit it, and returns the estimator as a short computer program. The program is built from a library of probability distributions. The returned law can therefore be a parametric distribution, a mixture or a multivariate factorization, with distribution parameters given by explicit formulas in the covariates. We call this approach agentic distributional regression (ADR). Unlike in the classical approach, the statistician no longer chooses the estimator, but asks an agent to build one. Treating the returned program as a random conditional density estimator, we derive a finite-sample error bound under assumptions on the number of admissible models and on the accuracy of the agent's fit, and an oracle inequality for the selection of a model among fitted candidates using independent validation data. Finally, assuming that, as the sample size grows, the agent selects the same smooth parametric model with probability tending to one and fits it accurately, we show that the estimated parameters are asymptotically normal. In simulation studies, on twelve real datasets and on a new dataset whose responses postdate the agents' training data, ADR with Claude Opus 5.5 has the best average performance among the existing methods from the statistical literature with which it is compared.

title: Energy equality and renormalization of Navier-Stokes-Vlasov equations
summary: We study weak solutions of the incompressible and the compressible Navier--Stokes--Vlasov systems on a bounded domain, where a viscous fluid is coupled to a dispersed particle phase through a drag force; the fluid obeys the no-slip boundary condition and the particles are subject to specular reflection. For solutions with Besov regularity, we show that the Vlasov equation is renormalizable in the sense of DiPerna--Lions, and we give regularity thresholds for the validity of the global energy equality. If the distribution function $f$ belongs to $B_p^{α,\infty}$ in space and velocity with time integrability $p$, and the fluid velocity $\mathbf{u}$ belongs to $B_q^{β,\infty}$ jointly in space and time with integrability $q$, then the energy equality holds provided $α+β>1$ and $β$ exceeds an explicit bound depending on $p$, $q$ and the dimension, under a natural integrability assumption on the pressure; an analogous criterion holds for the compressible system when the density is bounded from above and below. The condition $αp>1$ imposed on $f$ is not merely technical: it is exactly the range in which the macroscopic momentum flux possesses a boundary trace, so that the specular reflection condition passes to the macroscopic energy balance. When the particle phase is absent, our thresholds coincide with the criteria $β>\frac12+\frac1q$ and $β>\frac3q$ obtained by Yu for the incompressible Navier--Stokes equations alone. The proofs combine a boundary cutoff argument with commutator estimates based on a scale-localized Besov modulus, together with a boundary-strip analysis.

title: Evaluating AlphaEarth Embeddings for Crop Classification: Separability, Temporal Dynamics, and Cross-Regional Transferability
summary:
Earth Observation (EO)-based agricultural monitoring is shifting from pixel-level spectral analysis toward representation-driven modeling, yet systematic evaluation of learned representations remains limited. Geospatial foundation models (FMs) generate high-dimensional embeddings encoding complex spatio-temporal land-surface properties, but their utility and interpretability for agricultural applications remain insufficiently understood. This study presents a representation-agnostic framework evaluating a 64-dimensional AlphaEarth embedding space against Sentinel-2 reflectance, NDVI phenology, and harmonic features across geometric separability, temporal dynamics, spatial robustness, and cross-regional generalisation using field-scale data from the Conterminous United States (CONUS; 2017-2023) and Northern India (2021).
  Traditional features achieve strong linear separability (Fisher ratio), while embeddings provide superior distribution-aware separation - Bhattacharyya and Mahalanobis distances up to an order of magnitude higher for spectrally similar pairs (e.g. Corn/Soybeans: 3.9 vs. 0.10). Embeddings uniquely capture multi-year crop rotation dynamics, yielding a separability ratio of 1.784, versus a maximum of 1.003 for all engineered features. Under spatially explicit validation, embeddings exhibit lower residual spatial autocorrelation of errors (mean Moran's $I \approx 0.17$), reducing reliance on geographic proximity. However, harmonic features show stronger cross-continental transferability (US $\to$ India Macro F1: 0.493 vs. 0.326 for embeddings), with NDVI showing a similar advantage. The combined feature space yields balanced performance. These findings reveal a trade-off between representational richness and cross-region transferability, providing a framework for feature selection in large-scale crop classification.

title: Scale-aware and spatially-localised optimisation of kilometre-scale MLWP models
summary: Preserving fine-scale structure without degrading spatial accuracy is a central challenge for kilometre-scale machine-learning weather prediction (MLWP). We introduce a loss based on the dual-tree complex wavelet transform that constrains atmospheric fields jointly by scale, location, and orientation. We evaluate its performance using an experimental joint global--regional FastNet configuration, which produces \SI{1.5}{km} forecasts over the UK alongside $\sim$\SI{31}{km} global forecasts. Relative to both mean-squared error (MSE) and an FFT-based spectral objective, the wavelet loss substantially improves spectral fidelity. Compared with MSE training, it maintains similar pointwise performance, improves neighbourhood-based verification, and produces sharper precipitation fields with more realistic intensity distributions. These results demonstrate that spatially localised wavelet constraints can preserve multiscale atmospheric structure while largely avoiding the loss of pointwise accuracy associated with globally supported spectral objectives.

title: ETC-Bench: A Multilingual Benchmark for Evaluation-Side Transcript Canonicalization
summary: Written transcripts of the same speech can differ in ways that are not uniquely determined by the speech signal. We formulate evaluation-side transcript canonicalization (ETC), which maps multiple surface forms to a single canonical form when their differences are not determined by speech. To our knowledge, ETC-Bench is the first and most comprehensive multilingual benchmark for evaluation-side transcript canonicalization, covering 181 phenomenon types across 12 languages. Each instance is a minimal pair that shares a sentence context and differs only in a target span exhibiting one phenomenon. To evaluate both canonicalization success and semantic preservation, we propose Semantic-preserving Exact-match Normalization Accuracy (SENA), which combines exact agreement between independently canonicalized pair members with a pair-relative BERTScore constraint against information loss. We further introduce the Taxonomy-guided Agent Canonicalization Skill (TACS), which provides LLM agents with phenomenon descriptions and explicit canonicalization contracts. Experiments with five baseline configurations and three TACS-based agents show that the agents outperform the baseline systems on shared languages. ETC-Bench provides a systematic testbed for evaluation-side transcript canonicalization across languages.

title: Evaluation-Guided Demonstration Refinement for Vision-Language-Action Policies: The Winning Entry in the MetaFine Open Competition
summary: We fine-tuned a separate $π_{0.5}$ policy for each of the five tasks in the MetaFine Open Competition, with a task-specific training mixture and number of actions executed per prediction. Training started from the official demonstrations and expert procedures. Local evaluation exposed recurring grasping, pushing, and insertion failures. We addressed them by revising the demonstrated motions and by adding expert continuations from states the policy reached, while keeping nominal demonstrations in training. Checkpoints were compared on every instruction, so that a gain on one instruction could not hide a loss on another. Our submission, MAI, ranked first overall with a score of 96.66.

title: JevRec: Linguistic Encoding with Jev-like Decision Modeling for LLM-based Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommendation (GR) represents items as semantic identifiers (SIDs) and autoregressively generates the next item's SID from interaction history. However, most methods assign the same SID length to all items despite highly unequal interaction frequencies. This uniform design repeatedly incurs the cost of fine-grained codes for popular items, while shortening codes to reduce this cost also compresses the semantic representations of long-tail items. Inspired by the compact forms of frequent expressions in natural language, we propose JevRec to encode items as variable-length words and generate the next item from interaction context. Linguistic encoding retains frequency-dependent semantic prefixes from shared codebooks, producing shorter SIDs for popular items and richer descriptions for long-tail items. Yet predicting a sequence-level length and generating token-level content impose different optimization requirements that may conflict under a shared output head. Our Jev-like decision modeling component therefore predicts a length distribution with a dedicated head and generates content conditioned on length through a separate head while sharing the interaction-history representation. Experiments on three public datasets show that JevRec outperforms all compared baselines across the evaluated recommendation metrics. Further analyses show lower training and inference time than TIGER and reduced gradient conflict between length and content prediction.

title: API-TAIL: Detecting Model Substitution in LLM APIs through Temperature-Aligned Likelihood Tails
summary: Commercial language model APIs return only text, allowing a provider to cut costs by quietly routing a fraction of user requests to a cheaper substitute model while billing for the advertised one. Detecting such partial substitution is challenging because honest providers also alter the output distribution through undocumented decoding and serving choices, such as temperature scaling, sampling truncation, repetition and presence penalties, and default system prompts, forcing an audit to test against a composite null of legitimate configurations rather than a single reference. Our key insight is that these legitimate variations primarily shift response typicality across the entire batch, whereas partial substitution injects individual responses that remain anomalous under the claimed model. Building on this, we introduce API-TAIL, a typicality audit that first absorbs batch-level shifts by aligning a single effective temperature to center standardized surprisal scores across the audited batch, and then flags the endpoint if the number of remaining tail responses exceeds a threshold calibrated across legitimate configurations. Evaluated on real-world API responses and constructed substitution mixtures, API-TAIL controls false alarms across diverse honest providers and detects low-rate partial substitution with a small query budget. Under a common composite calibration, it outperforms the adapted rank- and MMD-based audit baselines.

title: Orthogonal and Parametrized Multi-Attribute Steering of LLMs
summary: Activation steering offers an effective and efficient way to modify an LLM's behavior at inference time. However, it remains unclear how to apply steering such that the signal is consistently strong and the steering strength has a universally interpretable meaning. We address this first by identifying the most steerable interval for each steering vector and rescaling the steering range accordingly. Building on this, we introduce a more interpretable method for steering, called parameterized steering which instead of pushing activations in a direction, it sets them at the desired trait strength. Next, with multi-trait steering, we find that naively combining vectors causes them to interfere with one another. In response, we develop a method to orthogonalize the vectors; it decouples these traits, allowing a model to exhibit one behavior without inducing the others, thus enabling multiple traits to be steered simultaneously.

title: REGER: Modeling inter-item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
summary: Personalized recommendation depends on learning semantic and collaborative relations among items from online content and user interactions. Generative recommendation (GR) offers a promising paradigm by autoregressively generating discrete semantic IDs (SIDs) of items. However, randomly initialized SID token embeddings and GR models trained from scratch do not directly inherit the semantic relations inherent in items, while inter-item collaborative relations are learned largely implicitly through token-level attention and next-token supervision. To address this limitation, we propose REGER, a unified framework that explicitly incorporates inter-item relations into semantic pretraining, history encoding, and SID generation. We pretrain the GR model through generative semantic retrieval, enabling it to inherit inter-item semantic similarity by learning to generate semantic neighbors' SIDs. We combine global attention with local attention aligned with SID boundaries to capture historical context and directed transitions between adjacent items. We further develop a theoretical framework for hierarchical preference decomposition over the SID prefix tree, proving an exact factorization of collaborative preference distributions and a weighted decomposition of item-level KL divergence into prefix-conditional KL divergences. Building on this analysis, we distill a discriminative teacher's full conditional distributions over all legal next tokens at ground-truth prefixes along the target SID path, jointly optimizing this objective with cross-entropy. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over existing GR baselines and support the effectiveness of the proposed preference distillation.

title: Near-quadratic sum-product estimates in fixed number fields
summary: Let $K$ be a fixed number field. We prove a quantitative expansion theorem for mixed sumsets $A+B$, assuming only that $A$ is covered by relatively few cosets of a multiplicative group of small finite valuation rank. The constants are independent of the generators, their heights, and their prime ideal supports. As a consequence, if $A\subset K^\times$, $|A|=N\ge 3$, and each element has nonzero valuation at at most $k$ finite places, then every $B\subset K$ with $|B|=N$ satisfies $$ \max\{|A+B|,|AA|\} \ge N^2\exp\left[-C_K\left((k+1)\log(\log N+2)+\sqrt{(k+1)\log N}\right)\right]. $$ This is $N^{2-o(1)}$ for $k=o(\log N/\log\log N)$. We also obtain a trade-off between the additive and multiplicative deficits, estimates for iterated linear sumsets, and a transfer theorem for product constructions $A=PG$ in terms of the multiplicative deficit of $P$. The proof recovers local scales from an exact sum and bounds the remaining conditional entropy by the overlap of entropy measures on fixed trees.

title: SpectRAG: Weighted Chunk Graphs for Token-Budgeted Context Selection in Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems ground large language models (LLMs) by retrieving external evidence and conditioning generation on the retrieved context. Although dense retrieval is effective for local semantic matching, independently ranked retrieval can return redundant passages, miss cross-chunk dependencies, and provide incomplete evidence for multi-hop reasoning. We propose SpectRAG, a spectral graph-augmented retrieval framework that combines hybrid candidate seeding, weighted chunk graph construction, graph-based expansion, spectral relevance propagation, and token-budgeted context selection. Document chunks are represented by dense semantic embeddings and graph-spectral coordinates derived from a weighted chunk graph whose edges encode semantic similarity, document adjacency, section hierarchy, shared entities, citation links, and similarity between LLM-generated utility questions. At query time, SpectRAG builds a high-recall seed set using exact inner-product search and hybrid relevance signals, expands it over the chunk graph, re-scores candidates using graph proximity and spectral information, and assembles the final context under a fixed token budget. The goal is not merely to retrieve individually similar chunks, but to construct a context that is relevant, diverse, structurally connected, and sufficient for grounded reasoning. Experiments on MultiHopRAG, UltraDomain, and long-document question-answering settings show that SpectRAG improves broad evidence recovery and achieves competitive generation quality against dense, hybrid, HyDE, LightRAG, and NaiveRAG baselines. The results further indicate that graph-spectral structure is particularly useful for inference-oriented and cross-document retrieval, while highlighting trade-offs in early precision, computational cost, and domain-dependent performance.

title: Noise Steering: Exploiting Wake Steering and Acoustic Directivity for Noise-Constrained Wind Farm Control via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Existing noise mitigation strategies for wind farms usually consist in reducing turbines power output, without accounting for the wake interactions between them and the noise emission directivity. This leads to over-conservative policies and unexploited wind power. Yet, turbine yaw can simultaneously affect wake interactions and the direction of noise emission, offering an additional degree of freedom for farm-level noise control. We therefore propose Noise Steering, a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) strategy that jointly controls turbine yaw angles and power setpoints to maximise farm power while satisfying a local noise constraint in a defined region. To enable training at a reduced computational cost, a low-fidelity acoustic model is coupled with the steady-state FLORIS simulator. The RL agent effectively learns how to redirect wakes and noise directivity away from the protected region while redistributing power across the farm. On a six-turbine test farm, the policy satisfies the 40 dB noise constraint throughout the full range of turbulent winds, with an average power deficit of only 2% relative to greedy unimpeded control, and up to 7.7% at high wind speeds. In comparison, the industry-standard noise-reduced operation (NRO) baseline here generates an average power loss of 17%. When deployed in the higher-fidelity FASTFarm simulator, the policy largely retains its performance under steady and turbulent inflow, despite differences in simulation fidelity. These results demonstrate the potential of combining yaw control and power derating through RL to improve the power-noise trade-off in wind farm operation.

title: Ego-CEVR: Learning Cross-Embodiment Visual Representations from Human Egocentric Videos
summary: As egocentric video becomes increasingly available for embodied learning, an important research question is how to turn this low-cost, scalable source of data into robot manipulation capabilities. Egocentric videos naturally provide rich context for high-level task understanding, while real-robot demonstrations with wrist observations and action annotations provide supervision for fine-grained action alignment. We present Ego-CEVR, a data-native framework for hierarchical visual representation learning that assigns distinct learning objectives to global and interaction representations. The global module learns object relations, task state, and temporal progress through future prediction on egocentric video. The Interaction module interprets wrist observations in global context and learns local alignment and contact cues through robot action supervision. Separate residual paths expose both representations to the action policy, preserving direct access to task context alongside fine-grained execution information. Ego-CEVR supports independent pretraining of its global video module on large-scale human egocentric videos and videos from diverse robot embodiments, without requiring robot action labels or paired wrist observations.

title: Uncovering Why LLMs Fail: From Internal Mechanisms to Adversarial Reasoning Trajectories
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are usually evaluated by final-output correctness or safety, yet an endpoint label does not reveal how a failure develops throughout the reasoning process. We therefore ask whether ordinary reasoning failures and adversarially induced failures can be characterized using the same internal coordinates. Towards this end, we in this paper study a white-box diagnostic framework CauTrace to disclose the root-cause of why LLM fails from three fundamental inspections: Functional States, Propagation of Representation, Temporal-State Coordination and Reasoning Trajectory. First, seven functional states are creatively defined to represent the support and constraint processing in LLMs. Second, the propagation of representation change measures how the changes among the seven states persist across subsequent Transformer blocks. Third, temporal-state coordination and trajectory topology characterize when the commitment and verification occur relative to the support, and how the dominant state sequence evolves over the full inference process. Finally, we evaluate CauTrace on both clean reasoning failures and paired adversarial perturbations. Across Qwen and LLaMA-family models, the failed traces show weaker Attention-MLP agreement on support-state updates and less verification activity relative to commitment, while the exact representation-level signatures and timing shifts vary by architecture. Held-out repair and steering tests demonstrate consistent operational signals that were in line with our claims for certain models and specific settings, with aligned steering producing the predicted directional changes in process measures. Overall, CauTrace provides a unified diagnostic framework for analyzing failure dynamics through changes in support, commitment, and verification, which would shed light on the in-depth research on LLM security.

title: TRIDENT-Seq: Profile-Matched Prefix-Future Contrast for Label-Efficient Payment Risk Modeling
summary: Ant International accumulates large volumes of transaction history across users and payment businesses. Confirmed fraud and chargeback outcomes, by contrast, are scarce, delayed, and specific to each business. A single encoder pretrained on unlabeled histories could serve all businesses, but only if pretraining captures the behavior that separates risk. Coarse activity differences can make contrastive pretraining on transaction logs too easy: transaction volume, amount, and timing can distinguish a history's continuation from arbitrary candidates without modeling how payment resources are used. We present TRIDENT-Seq, a transaction foundation model trained with Prefix-Future Contrast (PFC). PFC matches each prefix to a summary of its subsequent behavior among candidates with similar activity profiles; activity prediction and dispersion regularization act on the encoder output. Across three production payment businesses, the pretrained encoder improves average precision (AP) and recall at a 0.5% intervention budget over architecture-matched scratch training in all six business-budget settings. With a fixed validation set, it exceeds full-label scratch training in mean AP and recall using 10% of the training labels on Wallet and 25% on Shopping and SME. Pretraining only on another business's histories still helps. Replacing profile-matched candidates with random ones cuts recall from 24.62% to 5.64%. In Ant International's deployment evaluation, recorded amount-based chargeback and overall loss rates are 37.7% and 37.9% lower than those of the previous XGBoost-based system under the same intervention budget.

title: A sparse canonical Rado theorem
summary:
Canonical Ramsey theory studies structured colour patterns in colourings with arbitrarily many colours. Lefmann's canonical Rado theorem extends the canonical van der Waerden theorem of Erdős and Graham to partition-regular linear systems. Recently, Alvarado, Kohayakawa, Morris, Mota and Ortega proved a sparse canonical van der Waerden theorem for random set $[n]_p$.
  In this paper, we prove a sparse canonical Rado theorem. For every irredundant partition-regular matrix $A$ of positive rank with $k\ge3$ columns, and every prescribed partition witnessing the columns condition, if $p\ge Cn^{-1/m(A)}$, then with probability at least $1-e^{-cnp}$ every colouring of $[n]_p$ contains $$Ω\big(p^k n^{k-\rank(A)}\big)$$ canonical solutions of $A\mathbf x=0$ with distinct coordinates. A matching 0-statement holds when the prescribed partition has one or at least three blocks; the Schur equation shows that it can fail for two-block patterns. For every prescribed partition, we also establish a robust threshold at the same scale under deletion of a fixed positive proportion of the random set.

title: Progressively Refining SAM for Accurate Phytoplankton Segmentation
summary: Accurate phytoplankton segmentation is essential for ecological monitoring, yet it remains largely underexplored due to the subtle visual characteristics of phytoplankton and the scarcity of pixel-level annotations. To address these challenges, we propose PhySeg, a SAM-based segmentation framework equipped with a lightweight refinement module that progressively restores fine-grained details through multi-scale feature fusion. In addition, we construct a phytoplankton segmentation dataset by manually annotating instance-level masks for an existing dataset, providing a valuable resource for future research. Experimental results demonstrate that PhySeg improves segmentation accuracy, validating the effectiveness of the proposed module. Code is available at https://github.com/lijialin404/PhySeg.

title: Joint Distributional Copula Regression for Insurance Claim Frequency and Severity via Boosting
summary: In this paper, we introduce a model-based boosting approach for fitting structured additive distributional copula regression models for bivariate responses, with particular emphasis on jointly modeling insurance claim frequency and severity. The approach uses regression-type base learners, such as linear terms and splines with low degrees of freedom. It builds on generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS), which extend generalized additive models (GAMs) by allowing multiple distributional parameters, rather than only the conditional mean, to depend on covariates. The structured additive predictors make the model inherently interpretable, offering greater transparency and auditability than black-box approaches. These features are particularly relevant in regulated actuarial settings and applications requiring explainable artificial intelligence. By estimating the entire conditional joint distribution, the framework also enables insurance practitioners to examine conditional quantiles, tail behavior, and prediction intervals of risks. The copula component captures dependence between claim frequency and severity and allows practitioners to investigate how this dependence varies with policyholder characteristics, potentially improving predictive performance. Moreover, by incorporating modern machine-learning techniques, specifically boosting, the proposed model improves prediction accuracy while retaining interpretability. We assess the proposed framework using both simulated and real data. The results demonstrate its ability to recover the true covariate effects on the marginal distributional parameters and the dependence structure, select informative variables, and achieve predictive performance competitive with standard benchmark models. We also illustrate how to interpret the fitted model.

title: The scale of homogeneity in DESI Data Release 1
summary: We present measurements of the scale of cosmic homogeneity using the first data release (DR1) of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), the largest publicly available spectroscopic extragalactic survey to date. Using a counts-in-spheres estimator applied to nearly 5 million galaxies and quasars across six independent redshift bins spanning $0.1 < z < 2.1$, we measure the correlation dimension $D_2(r)$ and define the homogeneity scale $R_H$ as the point at which the galaxy distribution reaches within 1\% of the homogeneous asymptotic value. We find that all tracers clearly transition to homogeneity, with the galaxy homogeneity scale ranging from $93.8^{+0.9}_{-0.7}$ to $142.6^{+1.4}_{-1.4}$ $h^{-1}$Mpc depending on the tracer redshift, galaxy bias, and modelling used to extract the scale. Using a cosmology-dependent model, we reconstruct the underlying matter homogeneity scale, finding it decreases monotonically with redshift in excellent agreement with $Λ$CDM predictions. We identify a systematic offset of up to $\sim 10\%$ between measurements in the North and South Galactic Caps, largely due to fiber assignment effects reproduced in our simulations. Accounting for this, and with a complementary demonstration using toy models that our methodology correctly identifies inhomogeneous universes in all but rather finely-tuned observer configurations, this hence provides strong evidence in favour of the cosmological principle across our full redshift range. Our matter homogeneity scale measurements are consistent with, and substantially more precise than, previous constraints from WiggleZ and SDSS, demonstrating the power of DESI data for precision tests of the cosmological principle.

title: Interpretable Feature Discovery from Unstructured Data Using LLMs and Statistical Choice Models
summary: Feature extraction from unstructured data typically relies on opaque embeddings unsuited to interpretable decision-making. Interpretable features, on the other hand, typically require costly, and often infeasible, hand-engineering. Large language models (LLMs) offer a natural bridge, as they can read raw data and describe it in interpretable terms. One could simply ask an LLM to extract features from a large sample of the dataset, but context limitations and diluted attention can lead to unsatisfactory results. We introduce a method that automatically discovers interpretable, decision-relevant features from unstructured data. Our key idea is to perform pairwise comparisons between items, asking an LLM to articulate, in interpretable terms, the features distinguishing each pair. We treat these explanations, or rationales, as data: we develop a statistical choice model that combines these rationales across the comparisons to identify relevant features and estimate per-item, per-feature scores. We first test our method on a synthetic hiring dataset of cover letters with known ground-truth features and show that it significantly outperforms direct LLM feature extraction in feature recovery. We then apply it to the ChangeMyView (Reddit) debate dataset, where it discovers several interpretable features associated with persuasion while reaching predictive accuracy comparable to established baselines. We also show how the same rationales can be used to audit LLM decisions, yielding a holistic score whose decomposition over interpretable features reveals what the LLM rewards.

title: Neural Compression of Long ADMM Trajectory for Multiparametric Quadratic Program
summary: Solving large-scale multiparametric quadratic programs (mpQPs) in real time often requires thousands of iterative optimization updates, creating a major computational bottleneck in model predictive control and learning-enabled systems. This paper proposes TQPNet, a self-supervised neural compression framework that learns to compress long ADMM optimization trajectories into a compact neural warm start followed by a few refinement iterations. We derive a low-dimensional ADMM scheme operating on the primal-dual variables $(x,β)$ and show that its iteration admits an equivalent ReLU-layer representation, termed ADMM(ReLU). Building on this insight, TQPNet combines a multilayer perceptron with ReLU activations (MLP(ReLU)) and a small number of unrolled ADMM(ReLU) refinement layers. The network is trained offline using an optimality-condition-informed residual loss, eliminating the need for solver-generated labels. The proposed residual-based framework enables both self-supervised training and online solution certification through adaptive ADMM(ReLU) refinement. Experiments on large-scale mpQPs and real-time MPC applications demonstrate that TQPNet achieves high accuracy, strong generalization, and substantially faster inference than conventional optimization-based methods.

title: Prompt Lottery in LLM-as-a-Judge: Measuring and Mitigating Sensitivity to Syntactic Rephrasing
summary: LLM-as-a-Judge has become a standard for evaluating large language models, yet most approaches implicitly assume that a single judge prompt functions as a stable evaluation instrument. Prior work has primarily explored deliberate prompt modifications such as scoring rubrics, role descriptions, or chain-of-thought reasoning in order to optimize accuracy. In contrast, we investigate whether validated prompt variants intended to preserve evaluation semantics while differing in surface realization (\textit{paraphrastic rephrasings}) yield consistent judgments under a fixed evaluation task. We introduce \textit{Prompt Lottery}, a phenomenon in which paraphrastic rephrasings produce different LLMaJ judgments. Across a large-scale study spanning diverse evaluation tasks, judge families, and model backbones, we find that these variations can alter evaluation outcomes and, in some settings, reverse relative model rankings. A user study with 10 human annotators shows that LLMaJ judges exhibit 6-9$\times$ larger agreement degradation under prompt rephrasings than humans, falling below the generally accepted threshold in usability studies. This indicates that single-prompt evaluation is insufficiently robust for model ranking. Finally, we show that multi-prompt aggregation substantially improves robustness by emphasizing judgments that remain consistent across prompt variants.

title: A Comparative Study of Parallel Implementations of Short-Time Fourier Transform
summary: The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) computes the Fourier transform of a short-duration window of a longer signal, which characterizes how a frequency changes over time. While the Fourier transform algorithms, particularly the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm, has been well developed to take advantage of parallel computing, there is limited work on understanding the performance of parallel short-time Fourier transform algorithms. In this study, two parallel short-time Fourier transform algorithms, one is FFT-based and the other a quasi-parallel feedforward algorithm, are implemented and analyzed in comparison with each other. It is found that while the quasi-parallel algorithm outperforms in runtime under low concurrency settings, the FFT-based algorithm scales better and has lower memory usage. For each algorithm, three parallel approaches, shared-memory, distributed-memory and hybrid distributed-shared-memory, are tested. Profiling results show that all implementations are compute bound except for the hybrid feedforward algorithm, and that the distributed-memory variants incur significantly higher communication cost. Overall, this study presents a deeper and more comprehensive analysis and demonstrates the defining characteristics of different families of parallel short-time Fourier transform algorithms, in which the FFT-based approach uses less memory while the quasi-parallel feedforward algorithm has lower runtime but higher serial fraction.

title: Physical Effects in the Vicinity of Black Holes
summary: General relativity, a theory that is already over a century old, is still the best theory that we have to describe the universe at energy scales where only the gravitational force is important. It has stood tall to any observational tests thrown at it since its inception, and it has remarkable predictive power when it is utilized to study and model astrophysical problems. It also continues to surprise us with its ability to generate new problems and insights that render themselves useful in the study of modern physics. This is especially highlighted by the transition of modern observational astronomy away from an electromagnetic radiation epoch, and into a new gravitational wave epoch. This thesis devotes its study to phenomena that can be analyzed within the framework of classical general relativity, but whose results may contain interesting implications for cosmological and black hole observations. (Full abstract can be found in document).

title: Understanding Post-Quantum Cryptography Adoption: Practices, Challenges, and Evolution in Open-Source Software
summary: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards establish algorithms for quantum-safe systems, but empirical evidence about how software projects implement and maintain PQC support remains limited. We investigate this implementation and maintenance work by mining 114,361 commits and 5,713 issues across 179 open-source repositories. We use human annotation and validated LLM classification to identify PQC algorithms in commits, classify their adoption status and deployment mode, and identify technical challenges in issue discussions. The commit classification for PQC algorithms reveals that 90% of commits concern maintenance of existing support. From the issue discussions, we construct an 11-category taxonomy of recurring technical challenges. Build, packaging, and dependency failures, along with functional defects, account for approximately half of categorized issues. To examine how PQC support evolves, we use time-series analysis and first implementations of individual algorithms within repositories around NIST standardization milestones. After the 2024 finalization, standardized algorithm names appeared in more than 80% of the PQC development changes analyzed, although earlier names such as Kyber continued to appear. Development activity increased over the observation period. Our milestone analysis, however, did not find a significant increase in first implementations. Migration plans should therefore account for sustained maintenance, prioritize build reliability and integration testing, and track both standardized and predecessor algorithm names. We make the dataset, taxonomy, annotations, and analysis pipeline publicly available.

title: Cooperative EV Charging Assignment Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: A Comparison of QMIX and Independent Q-Learning Under Urban Traffic Uncertainty
summary: The allocation of electric vehicles to public charging stations is increasingly constrained by the fact that several heterogeneous facilities often serve the same stream of requests while observing only partial local information. An accept/reject decision that is defensible for one station may nevertheless reduce the efficiency of the charging district as a whole. We formulate this operational problem as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) and examine whether Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE), instantiated through QMIX, improves assignment performance relative to a cooperative Independent Q-Learning baseline (IQL). The evaluation uses a six-station urban network simulated with SUMO, five independent random seeds, 200 training episodes, and four traffic flux scenarios ranging from 100 to 250 vehicles/hour. Under this protocol, QMIX reaches a mean reward per evaluated decision of +0.776, versus +0.578 for IQL (delta = +0.198, seed-paired Cohens dz = 2.98, exact two-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.0625, the minimum attainable value at this sample size), and raises the acceptance rate from 72.4% to 94.0% (delta = +21.6 pp, dz = 5.24, Wilcoxon p = 0.0625). A five-variant ablation suggests this gain is primarily attributable to the CTDE architecture when holding cooperative reward terms fixed, though not formally isolated with a single seed. By contrast, cooperative reward shaping and experience sharing show no clear descriptive benefit and may slightly reduce performance. These findings support the view that, for multi-station charging assignment, coordination should be embedded in the learning architecture rather than added only through heuristic cooperation terms.

title: Perspective on AI and quantum open-source software
summary: Quantum open-source software provides essential infrastructure for quantum science, and artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping its capabilities and transforming its development. However, verifying quantum software at scale remains difficult, and AI-generated contributions can increase the workload of maintainers. In this Perspective, we examine verification as a central requirement for reliable AI-assisted quantum software development and research. We analyze public repositories, records covering 110 repositories from five annual quantum open-source hackathons that we organize, and responses from more than 1600 participants in a community survey. Our analysis connects limitations in automated verification with the review burden on quantum software maintainers. We propose verification practices and contribution standards that require contributors to support their changes with reproducible evidence for maintainer review. We also examine how quantum open-source software can provide infrastructure for AI-driven research whose results the community can independently verify and build upon. We maintain an open-source companion repository to support reproducibility and help projects adopt and refine these proposals. Together, these contributions help the quantum open-source software community translate advances in AI into reliable quantum research through reproducible verification.

title: PromptSense: Sentiment-Aware Mental Health Chatbot with Dynamic Prompting
summary: Current Large Language Models (LLMs)-based mental health chatbots often lack sufficient empathy, contextual awareness, and safety mechanisms, potentially leading to ineffective or harmful interactions. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates sentiment and depression analysis with a rule-based filtering mechanism prior to model inference. By dynamically constructing prompts based on emotional and risk-related insights, the framework aims to significantly improve the contextual relevance, empathy, and risk-aware of model-generated responses. We evaluated four model strategies and two prompt engineered variants across qualitative metrics such as empathy, helpfulness, clarity, relevance, safety, as well as toxicity assessments using the Perspective API. Experimental results indicate that the prompt engineering approaches outperforms DSFT and RLAIF by 1.8\% and 1.1\% respectively.

title: Evolutionary Demographics of Molecular Ice Mantles in Young Stars with SPHEREx
summary: Molecular ices are a primary reservoir of volatile C, O, and N in star-forming environments, tracing the chemical pathway from molecular clouds to planet-forming disks. SPHEREx provides contiguous 0.75--5~$μ$m all-sky spectrophotometry for vastly larger samples than are accessible to JWST, enabling population-scale ice demographics for the first time. We present a search for ice signatures in SPHEREx spectra of 20{,}292 young stellar objects (age $<20$~Myr) drawn from the Gaia-based kinematic catalog of Kounkel \& Covey 2019. Using laboratory templates for the spectral signatures of H$_2$O (3.05~$μ$m), CO$_2$ (4.27~$μ$m), and CO (4.67~$μ$m), we identify 746 H$_2$O ice candidates, including 131 high-confidence H$_2$O+CO$_2$ detections and 22 with additional corroborating CO absorption. When binning by age, we find that the H$_2$O$+$CO$_2$ detection rate declines by an order of magnitude between $\lesssim$3~Myr and $\sim$5~Myr, suggesting a chemical or physical evolutionary trend. Candidates concentrate toward high-extinction sightlines ($A_G \gtrsim 2.5$~mag) and embedded SED morphologies, consistent with the idea of envelope dispersal and photodesorption depleting detectable ice mantles within the first few million years of pre-main-sequence evolution. This catalog provides a homogeneous demographic baseline and a prioritized target list for JWST follow-up.

title: Reusable LLM-Based Plans with Probabilistic Guarantees for Self-Adaptive Systems
summary: Self-adaptive systems are designed to accommodate variants of their environment, which form a family of instances whose uncertainty is captured by probabilistic models, and must meet probabilistic requirements on each instance. Within such a family, changes in size and structure complicate the fundamental adaptation decision: whether to retain, reuse, or construct a new controller, since controllers are often synthesized for and specific to an instance. Large language models (LLMs) have recently been used to write reusable controllers, but existing approaches largely target deterministic domains, and probabilistic model checking of their output remains limited to preliminary single-instance studies. In this paper, we propose a verifier-guided framework for controller reuse with explicit support for families of environments. The framework introduces a novel combination of LLM-written controllers with probabilistic model checking to provide per-instance guarantees for probabilistic requirements. We evaluate our approach using three LLMs on three benchmarks, assessing its effectiveness and cost with respect to baseline implementations, the distribution of adaptation decisions, and the impact of individual framework components. On grid worlds, LLM-written rule lists are verified on about 90% of held-out instances, against at most 77% for the baselines, and verifying a stored rule list is 15 to 103 times faster than per-instance synthesis. Reuse serves most episodes at a small fraction of the cost of generation or per-instance synthesis, and model-checking feedback increases verified coverage over independent restarts.

title: Efficient Deep Gaussian Process Surrogates via Mini-Batch Latent MAP Estimation
summary: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are flexible surrogate models for computer experiments with nonstationary response surfaces, but inference over their latent representations remains computationally challenging. Existing methods typically rely on variational inference or Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which impose variational-family assumptions or require costly posterior sampling. We propose the latent maximum-a-posteriori deep Gaussian process (LaMP-DGP), which uses gradient-based optimization to obtain MAP estimates of the latent representations and enables efficient probabilistic prediction through linked-GP calculations. To scale LaMP-DGP to large datasets, we develop a mini-batch optimization algorithm and, under a polynomial mini-batch bias-decay condition, establish a stationarity bound for latent-state optimization that motivates a growing batch-size schedule. Across numerical experiments and real-data analyses, LaMP-DGP provides consistently competitive predictive performance relative to doubly stochastic variational inference, stochastic gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, and fully Bayesian Vecchia DGP inference. Computationally, LaMP-DGP is substantially faster than the Vecchia MCMC approach while remaining broadly competitive with the stochastic-gradient alternatives. These results position LaMP-DGP as a competitive and computationally efficient alternative for DGP inference. An R package, "LaMPDGP", is available for implementing the proposed method.

title: Measuring Deep Learning Performance - An Empirical Study of Performance Distributions Across Architectures and Tasks
summary: Context: Non-determinism in deep learning algorithm design and implementation leads to performance variation, meaning model performance is not a single value, but rather a distribution. These model performance distributions are underexplored despite their impact on robustness. Objective: We investigate the robustness of deep learning performance to sources of non-determinism, specifically focusing on how performance distributions differ across various architectures and tasks. Method: We conducted 186 experiments on image classification and time series forecasting architectures. Each experiment was run 100 times with different random seeds to generate performance distributions, resulting in 18,600 runs. Robustness was quantified using metrics for spread, symmetry, and tail risk. Results: Performance distributions are frequently non-Gaussian, particularly in time series forecasting. Model size does not systematically affect robustness -- larger image classification models show fewer outliers but not lower spread, while smaller time series models show lower spread but more extreme underperformers. Training duration does not scale linearly; early stopping effectively balances performance and robustness. Mean performance does not predict robustness - time series forecasting shows moderate correlation while image classification shows none. Time series models produce nearly three times more underperforming outliers than image classification models, indicating substantially higher tail risk. Conclusions: Tail risk poses serious concerns for Trustworthy AI in high-stakes applications. Models performing well on average may exhibit long tails and extreme outliers revealed only through distributional analysis. Mean performance alone should not guide model selection; assessment of spread, symmetry, and tail risk is essential for reliable model assessment where consistent performance is critical.

title: Tidal shells as clocks of galaxy mergers and tests of cosmological models
summary: Stellar shells-concentric arc-like tidal features formed in galaxy mergers-provide a valuable record of recent galaxy assembly histories encoding both the merger event and the gravitational potential of the host galaxy. We compare shell systems in observations and cosmological simulations from two complementary perspectives. First, we show that simulations predict a substantial population of very large (>100kpc) shells that are rarely observed, revealing a potentially important discrepancy between simulations and reality. Because the scales of observed and simulated shell systems differ significantly, we focus on a comparison of merger histories. Using a shell-identification method, we estimate merger times for a sample of nearby massive prolate rotators and compare them with merger histories derived from cosmological simulations. We also present ongoing efforts to expand the sample of deeply imaged prolate rotators using observations from the Milankovic telescope, paving the way for future studies based on larger observational samples.

title: Learning from Relative Action Credit for Escaping Local Minima
summary: Reinforcement learning holds the promise of robots that learn manipulation skills from interaction alone, without pretrained priors or demonstration data. In practice, on-policy methods such as PPO routinely stall on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks: dense reward shaping carries the policy through stages, yet stitching them together and discovering sparsely rewarded events rarely succeeds. We trace this failure to the missing action discrimination in state-value credit assignment: a state-value critic judges progress only by episode outcomes, so when the policy converges to a partial solution all outcomes coincide, and improvement stops because no action can prove better than another. We therefore extend PPO with an action conditioned value critic which, can compare the executed action with alternatives sampled at the same state and aid the learning signal. Combined with Generalized Advantage Estimation and a bound on exploration noise, we show how the extended algorithm escapes the plateau and completes precise peg insertion within a training budget where PPO with identical exploration fails.

title: Why does the detonation cell size $λ$ provide quasi-universal scaling of detonation dynamics?
summary: The detonation cell size $λ$ is known to provide a characteristic scale for the detonation dynamics and serves as scaling parameter for numerous correlations with other dynamic parameters of detonations, e.g., the critical detonation tube diameter for transmission to open space of $d\simeq13λ$ across many reactive systems. In the present paper, we address the reason why such scaling works so well. We formulate a macroscopic reaction rate model for cellular detonations relying on the distribution of ignition delays in cellular detonations, conditioned by $λ$. The ignition delay distribution is modeled in terms of the cellular dynamics, using the closed form model recently proposed by Radulescu (JFM 2025) for the lead shock dynamics in a unit cell. The distribution of ignition delays obtained in closed form serves as a simple model for the phase-averaged reaction rate in a cell-averaged description. The global reaction rate model is applied to the problem of globally curved cellular detonations. Excellent agreement with experiment is obtained. The paper thus highlights for the first time a simple dynamic closure for cellular detonations and provides the simple answer why the cell size provides the relevant length scale for detonations: it provides the length of the mean detonation structure, or its hydrodynamic thickness.

title: Sample Complexity for Generative Learning of Quantum Measurement Data
summary: Generative learning of a quantum measurement distribution from finite data requires choosing a model capacity that balances representation accuracy against estimation cost. We develop a bias-variance framework that decomposes the expected population Kullback-Leibler error at model capacity $s$ and sample size $N$ as $\mathcal E(s,N)=B(s)+V(s,N)$, with representation bias $B$ and a variance term $V$ capturing the mean estimation error. In the well-sampled regime, $V(s,N)\simeq[NC(s)]^{-1}$, and exponential or algebraic laws for $B$ and $C$ yield four scaling templates for the optimal error, from inverse powers of $N$ to inverse powers of $\ln N$. For local autoregressive models, the context radius sets the model capacity, and $B$ is the summed conditional mutual information lost by truncating the context. For a smoothed histogram learner, we derive an exact finite-sample estimation cost that accounts for rarely observed contexts and recovers the parameter-count law in the well-sampled regime. For transverse-field Ising Born distributions, the independently evaluated bias and estimation cost predict both the optimal context radius and the optimal error. In the well-sampled regime, the estimation cost grows exponentially with context radius. Its competition with approximately exponential bias decay in the gapped regimes predicts power-law error decay in $N$, while algebraic bias decay at criticality predicts asymptotic inverse-power decay in $\ln N$. Bulk-site results are consistent with the corresponding finite-sample predictions. These results connect the structure of quantum measurement distributions to the model capacity justified by finite data.

title: Assessing Language Models for Scientific Applications: Inertial Confinement Fusion as a Use Case
summary: Advancing language models for specialized scientific applications requires evaluations of scientific fluency, physical reasoning, and quantitative analyses. Using inertial confinement fusion (ICF) as a test case, we have developed an expert-curated benchmark of 250 questions spanning qualitative reasoning, numerical calculation, symbolic derivation, and equation formulation. Responses have been evaluated using deterministic numerical and symbolic checks together with language-model judges. We compared a variety of out-of-the-box closed-source and open-source large language models with Prospero, a model specialized through combined domain-adaptive pretraining and supervised fine-tuning for ICF. We also conducted initial retrieval-assisted evaluations. Prospero improved its aggregate score by 10.7 percentage points over its base model, with gains across all question types. Frontier models achieved the highest aggregate scores, but critical physics errors persisted, particularly in numerical calculations. We note that domain-specific performance can improve through specialization, but benchmark gains alone do not establish scientific reliability. Retrieval improved performance for a smaller model but yielded no statistically significant improvement for a frontier model. Two scientific stress tests further illustrate useful capabilities and the need for expert assessment of physical assumptions and model validity. Based on these findings, we recommend evaluating existing domain capabilities and retrieval benefits before committing to substantial additional specialization.

title: Where Can We Fool the Model's Mind? Response-Guided Semantic Probing and Adaptive Routing for Transferable Attacks on Black-Box MLLMs
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) ground language in visual evidence, yet their semantic reasoning can be exploited through transferable black-box adversarial attacks. Existing attacks typically allocate perturbations using surrogate-model saliency, which may not reflect how an unseen MLLM semantically interprets or relies on different image regions. We introduce VISTA (Vulnerability-Informed Semantic Transfer Attacks), a black-box framework that identifies semantically vulnerable visual regions from an MLLM's responses without access to gradients, logits, parameters, or internal representations. VISTA supports two attack settings: (i) VISTA-Proxy, a pure-transfer setting that probes an open-source MLLM and transfers the resulting adversarial examples to unseen commercial MLLMs without querying them; and (ii) VISTA-Victim, a query-assisted setting that probes the target MLLM to capture model-specific semantic vulnerabilities. VISTA builds an Uncertainty-Based Multimodal Behavior (UBMB) map from response drift, conflict, misleading, and semantic shifts, then uses entropy-adaptive Sinkhorn routing and a surrogate ensemble to focus perturbations on vulnerable regions. Across GPT-5, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and Claude Sonnet 4.6, VISTA achieves up to 97 % attack success rate (ASR) while maintaining a Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) above 30 dB. Notably, VISTA-Proxy achieves up to 93 % ASR without querying the final victim, demonstrating that response-derived semantic vulnerability can enable effective transfer across heterogeneous MLLMs.

title: Finite-step statistical mechanics of scale-invariant learning: spectral equations of state and curvature transport
summary: Stationary learning admits an ideal-gas description under restrictive noise assumptions. In neural networks whose gradient noise departs from these assumptions, however, an entropy-scaling relation resembling a Maxwell relation remains approximately valid. We ask which thermodynamic-looking relations follow from scale symmetry rather than equilibrium, and how departures from the ideal-gas description can be quantified, for discrete stochastic gradient dynamics with memory. An exact rescaling of trajectories explains the entropy relation without assuming thermal equilibrium. Within a local harmonic approximation, self-adjusting weight norms yield a spectral equation of state whose virial coefficients are set by moments of the curvature spectrum, and coupled parameter groups can sustain stationary probability currents. Our central result beyond this approximation is an exact curvature-transport identity. Together with a finite-step loss balance, it decomposes corrections to the harmonic fluctuation relation into measurable curvature changes, finite-step remainders, gradient-memory correlations and finite-window drift terms. A related displacement-weighted curvature change provides a diagnostic of the arrow of time; its mean and second moment give a lower bound on the relative entropy between forward and reversed state pairs. We also calculate the activation-boundary contribution to curvature for rectified teacher-student networks with Gaussian inputs. Tests in sphere models, teacher-student networks and convolutional networks on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 support the transport description and identify limits of the harmonic and cubic-remainder approximations. These results separate symmetry-based relations from equilibrium assumptions and provide quantitative diagnostics of nonideal fluctuations in learning dynamics.

title: An Optimal Seed Reveals the Dynamical Route to Spontaneous Splitting of Turbulent Puffs
summary: The localized turbulence in pipe flow, known as puffs, is sustained by their proliferation. This process is crucial to the subcritical laminar-turbulent transition, a century-old fundamental problem related to a wide range of natural and engineered systems. Here, we leverage the nonlinear nonmodal analysis of a reduced-order model to capture the full Navier-Stokes dynamics of the splitting process: from the splitting seed through the edge state to successful splitting, even when the pre-edge evolution is obscured by the puff's intrinsic chaotic fluctuations. Moreover, the optimized evolution provides a splitting-progress coordinate to frame a phase-space representation of the proliferation, resolving the temporal desynchronization among chaotic realizations and thereby enabling dynamically aligned ensemble averaging to uncover the underlying splitting dynamics. The splitting seed is characterized by a strong velocity inflection, and its energy threshold exhibits a power-law scaling with the Reynolds number, giving the optimal solution direct physical consistency in spontaneous puff splitting.

title: Large Language Models for Accurate Medical Chart Abstraction: Enabling Scalable and Secure Artificial Intelligence Deployment in Stroke
summary: Medical chart abstraction transforms unstructured clinical narratives into structured variables for research and quality monitoring. We evaluated a prompting-based large language model (LLM) framework for extracting eight clinical variables from 2,416 neurointerventional acute stroke intervention reports across three hospitals. Twenty-two instruction-tuned open-source LLMs were evaluated across architectures, model sizes, and biomedical adaptations using Quick Response and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting. Non-expert staff annotations served as the cross-model reference standard. Evaluation was restricted to report-variable pairs with a valid LLaMA3.3-70B CoT prediction and a corresponding reference label. Performance measures included extraction accuracy, inference latency, and agreement with expert adjudication. Twenty discordant cases per variable underwent review by two senior physicians and four medical students. LLaMA3.3-70B achieved the highest overall accuracy (94.8%). CoT improved performance on inference-dependent variables such as site of occlusion, while Quick Response was optimal for directly stated procedural fields. Expert adjudication showed that AI predictions were more closely aligned with expert interpretations than non-expert annotations for most variables, with intracranial angioplasty remaining a challenge. Locally deployed LLMs can support scalable clinical information extraction and retrospective stroke registry curation, with expert oversight for ambiguous cases.

title: Are Seismic Foundation Models More Than Glorified Feature Extractors?
summary: Earthquake sequences are stochastic on two separated timescales: the seismic waves of any individual earthquake propagate over seconds to minutes, while the earthquakes themselves arrive as a sparse, self-exciting occurrence process, with inter-event intervals from seconds to months. Respecting both scales in one training objective is the open challenge. Foundation models (FMs) for seismic waveforms instead import their learning targets from audio and vision, where every target is computed from a single fixed-length window. Such a window holds one realization of the wave propagation (an earthquake trace), never the occurrence process that decides when earthquakes happen. We develop nine model designs sharing one Mamba encoder-decoder, trained on a fixed corpus of 3M windows, varying the self-supervised objective, quantization bottleneck and mixer; the two key comparisons are architecture-matched, varying the objective alone. Each checkpoint is evaluated frozen on three downstream tasks. Varying the target redistributes downstream skill rather than raising it, and no checkpoint wins everywhere. Adding masking pressure to our strongest classifier re-specializes it rather than making it a generalist: it gains 6.9 points of few-shot P-wave picking precision and loses 9.6 points of few-shot classification accuracy. By the standard imported from language and vision, these models are feature extractors rather than FMs. Controls on capacity, architecture, and domain proximity do not explain why skill moves rather than rises. Against task-specific baselines the advantage is regime-dependent: our checkpoints beat them few-shot on classification and ground-motion prediction, and trail them on full data. We argue the binding constraint is the target, and that settling the question requires a learning target defined across events, the timescale that makes seismicity stochastic in the first place.

title: New Multiple Descent Phenomena Induced by Heterogeneous Data
summary: Modern machine learning models are often trained on large datasets assembled from many different sources, whose statistical properties can differ substantially. Understanding how this heterogeneity affects generalization performance is therefore important for explaining how model performance changes as model size increases. In this work, we study this question in linear random-feature models and show that mixtures of datasets with different covariance structures can give rise to a range of multiple-descent phenomena. We derive exact asymptotic expressions for the test error of each data source in the high-dimensional regime, and show how heterogeneity in covariance scale and spectral structure can introduce additional, group-dependent interpolation thresholds as model size increases. These phenomena arise even with noiseless labels and linear activations, showing that neither label noise nor activation nonlinearity is necessary for multiple-descent. Our results therefore provide a different perspective from classical explanations of multiple descent. More broadly, our results have potential implications for algorithmic fairness by showing that model scaling can affect different data groups unevenly, amplifying disparities in their generalization errors. We validate our theoretical results on synthetic Gaussian mixtures and real-world datasets, including MNIST and CIFAR-10.

title: Preserving Safety During Sequential Fine-Tuning: A Factorial and Geometric Analysis of Replay
summary: Benign fine-tuning can erode safety alignment in large language models, and sequential adaptation substantially compounds this risk. Prior work mitigates this erosion by replaying harmful-prompt refusals and benign-compliance examples, while other work instead matches base-model logits via distillation. However, the individual contributions of supervised exposure and distillation to safety behavior and refusal geometry during sequential adaptation remain unclear. We factor these two strategies apart and study their behavioral and geometric effects during sequential LoRA fine-tuning of Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B across diverse task sequences (code generation, German-language summarization, and science question-answering). Behaviorally, supervised replay exposure yields the largest reduction in HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) on Mistral, averaging 51.1 points below base, but at a substantial over-refusal cost, averaging 53.4 points above base on OR-Bench-hard. Logit distillation, without any supervised replay loss, largely prevents safety erosion at a fraction of this cost: an average 5.4-point ASR reduction against only a 5.1-point rise in over-refusal. Llama shows the same asymmetry between the two strategies. Combining exposure and distillation moderates exposure's over-refusal while leaving downstream task scores largely unaffected. Geometrically, the two models diverge: on Mistral, distillation preserves the base refusal direction more closely than exposure does, whereas on Llama, refusal behavior after exposure largely survives ablation of the extracted refusal direction. This dissociation between models indicates that preserving the base refusal direction is not a reliable proxy for behavioral safety.

title: Self-Labeled Preference Transfer for Steerable Robot Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can learn to follow execution preferences, such as where to grasp an object or how to move around an obstacle, from demonstrations annotated with preference labels. Providing these annotations for every new task, however, is costly. We study whether learned preference control can transfer to new tasks whose demonstrations contain the desired behaviors but lack preference annotations. We find that a policy trained with preference annotations can follow preferences on a new task before adaptation but achieves limited task success. Fine-tuning on target demonstrations without these annotations improves task success while weakening preference control. Motivated by this finding, we introduce Self-Labeled Preference Transfer (SPT). SPT jointly trains a shared vision-language backbone for preference-conditioned action prediction and preference recognition on annotated source demonstrations. It then freezes the recognizer to preserve its cross-task preference recognition capability and uses it to self-label target demonstrations for policy fine-tuning. Across five types of execution preferences in simulation, the recognizer achieves 96.4% accuracy, and SPT reaches 84.8% preference following and 89.2% task success, compared with 59.4% and 88.0% for naive finetuning. We further extend to multiple preferences, achieving 93.8% preference following compared with 42.5% of baselines. In real-world experiments, SPT increases preference following from 52.5% to 92.5% relative to naive finetuning across two task transfers. These results show that SPT can support preference adaptation across tasks and objects while maintaining success, without additional manual preference annotations.

title: Inexact PDHG for Large-Scale Semidefinite Programming
summary: First-order methods, such as the primal-dual hybrid gradient (PDHG) method, have recently been explored for large-scale semidefinite programming (SDP). However, exact projections can be computationally prohibitive, motivating inexact projections using conditional gradient methods. Although computationally cheap and projection-free, these methods typically converge sublinearly. Recent variants, such as Spectrahedron Frank-Wolfe (Garber, 2026), achieve linear convergence in expectation near the optimal face of the spectrahedron. We develop an inexact PDHG framework with tractable spectrahedral projections using two techniques: (i) adaptive error tolerances that avoid unnecessary inner iterations while guaranteeing convergence, and (ii) a heuristic spectral warm start based on the Lanczos algorithm that accelerates Spectrahedron Frank-Wolfe by initializing near the optimal face. We establish an O(1/t) convergence rate for PDHG in the presence of projection errors and estimate the total number of inner iterations required for convergence. Experiments on large-scale SDP instances demonstrate that combining spectral warm starts with Spectrahedron Frank-Wolfe outperforms Lanczos-based inexact projections.

title: Towards Generalizing Pretrained All-Atom Representations to Unified Binder Design
summary: PairFormer-based all-atom models demonstrate strong capabilities in biomolecular binder design. However, existing methods often use all-atom representations for modality-specific binder design, such as protein and peptide design. In contrast, recent geometric latent diffusion models pursue unified binder design by representing molecular blocks from different modalities in a shared latent space. These complementary strengths motivate us to investigate how to generalize the use of pretrained all-atom representations to unified binder design. We introduce PairFuse, a parameter-efficient method that enables this generalization through representation fusion. Specifically, we use lightweight layerwise adapters to integrate pretrained all-atom representations into an independently pretrained geometric latent diffusion model. Our adapters integrate pretrained all-atom representations through two mechanisms: enriching the diffusion model's molecular block features and incorporating pairwise structural information into the geometric diffusion model's denoiser. Theoretically, we prove that the augmented denoiser preserves geometry and pairwise attention fusion provides additional attention expressivity beyond feature-only fusion. Experimentally, across antibody, peptide, and small molecule binder-design benchmarks, PairFuse achieves stronger performance than the pretrained diffusion model and existing representation-fusion baselines.

title: GAUSS: A Workload-Aware Analytical and Monte-Carlo Simulator for LLM Inference Serving
summary: Large language model (LLM) inference has become an operational workload that fleets must provision, monitor, and bill against latency service-level objectives (SLOs). A single throughput number cannot answer the questions operators actually face, because generative serving couples two phases with very different service characteristics, continuous batching reshapes the effective service process, and user-visible tail latency can degrade long before aggregate throughput saturates. We present GAUSS, a workload-aware analytical and Monte-Carlo simulator that predicts the full distributions of time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-between-tokens (TBT), together with the sustainable request rate, for a given workload, engine, and accelerator. GAUSS pairs calibrated, phase-specific latency surfaces for prefill and decode with a Lindley-recurrence model of queueing under stochastic arrivals and estimates performance by ensemble Monte-Carlo sampling rather than by replaying a single trace. This lets GAUSS reason about workloads, routing policies, and hardware that have never been deployed, and to capture the latency tails that trace-driven simulators systematically under-sample. We describe the model and show how it supports operating-point selection, traffic segmentation, and shortest-remaining-processing-time scheduling capacity questions that trace-driven simulators cannot address.

title: Opening Rankings from Engine Self-Play Are Less Certain Than They Look: Sampling Error, Draws, and Strength Dependence in Strength-Limited Stockfish Games
summary: Engine self-play allows chess openings to be compared under controlled conditions, without the selection effects of human game databases. When openings differ only slightly, however, rankings built from a few hundred games can be unstable. In Study 1, strength-limited Stockfish 15.1 played 17,400 games: ten forced White first moves and ten forced Black replies to 1.e4, each at three strength settings. The leading opening changed between settings, twice by a single game. There was no statistically reliable evidence, though, that differences among openings depended on strength (White p = .311, Black p = .843). The design had limited sensitivity to isolated strength-dependent effects: a 12-point effect was detected by the omnibus test in only about 39% of simulated studies. A Connect Four positive control detected an observed 22.5-point center-column advantage, demonstrating sensitivity to large opening differences. With 290 games per opening, the observed leader was the true best of ten openings in only about 44% of simulated studies assuming a between-opening standard deviation of three percentage points. Follow-up studies with complete game records showed that the settings were ordered in direct matches but did not form a consistent Elo scale, that win and draw rates differed across hardware and implementation configurations, and that an apparent 1.d3 weakness was not confirmed in new games. With Stockfish 19 and a fixed node budget, survey-selected replies showed no statistically reliable advantage over free engine choice. Opening leaderboards from a few hundred engine games can overstate certainty.

title: Who Else Is In? Multi-Agent Collusion Initation Via Strategic Vagueness
summary: Multi agent LLM systems raise the risk of collusion among agents pursuing objectives hidden from their overseers.
